tagline: A planned desert town meets dunes made from volcanic ash and pumice.
intro: The Christmas Valley Back Country Byway runs 93 miles into Oregon’s high desert. The Bureau of Land Management presents the route as a way to reach geological features, from dunes of volcanic ash and pumice to an eroded volcano. The Black Hills Interpretive Site offers a parking area and an interpretive sign, reached on foot or by four-wheel-drive vehicle.

The settlement along the way took shape as a planned community after World War II. In 1961, developer M. Penn Phillips laid out Christmas Valley with holiday street names, an airport, a water system and an artificial lake. He marketed the land to prospective farmers and retirees in California, offering bus tours and flights. The parcels sold quickly, but few buyers moved there. The holiday theme had an older naming history behind it: Christmas was a corruption of Christman, the name of stockman Peter Christman, who grazed cattle in the area.

The byway begins at Oregon 31 and County Road 5-10. Christmas Valley provides a town anchor before the dunes to its east. Beyond the dunes lies Lost Forest Research Natural Area; Fossil Lake lies to their west. The dunes themselves reach 60 feet high, built largely from the eruption that formed Crater Lake.

moments.title: Christmas Valley
moments.text: Candy Lane and Mistletoe Road were part of M. Penn Phillips’s 1961 plan for Christmas Valley. The townsite also included an airport, golf course and artificial lake. Phillips sold California buyers the prospect of readily farmed land, but few took up residence. The community is now largely devoted to alfalfa farming. Its lake, originally Christmas Valley Lake, is called Baert Lake. Baert Lake is artificial, with part of its shoreline bordering the golf course. The Christmas Valley Park and Recreation District manages it, keeping one element of the planned town in recreational use.

moments.title: Crack in the Ground
moments.text: Crack in the Ground marks the western edge of a depression formed when older rock sank during eruptions from Four Craters Lava Field. The volcanic fissure extends about two miles, with depths nearly 30 feet below ground level. It lies at the lava field’s southwest corner.

moments.title: Christmas Valley Sand Dunes
moments.text: These dunes owe much of their material to Mount Mazama, the volcano whose eruption formed Crater Lake. Wind carried ash and pumice into this area 7,000 years ago. The dune complex covers 11,000 acres of public land and reaches heights of 60 feet. In 1983, the Bureau of Land Management combined the dunes, Lost Forest Research Natural Area and Fossil Lake into one Area of Critical Environmental Concern. That shared management area encompasses contrasting neighbors: Fossil Lake west of the dunes and Lost Forest to the east. The Bureau of Land Management administers all three.
moments.notice: The dunes reach heights of 60 feet.
